items.stem: The engraving below was published in 1591, based on drawings of Indigenous people in North America. It shows men and women planting seeds of beans and maize in cleared fields. Which conclusion about Native American societies before sustained European contact is best supported by this image?

stimulus.image_caption: Engraving by Theodor de Bry (1591), after drawings by Jacques Le Moyne de Morgues, showing Florida Indians planting seeds of beans and maize.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1591 engraving; pre-1930, public domain (Library of Congress)

options: (A) All Native Americans in every region depended entirely on hunting and gathering for food.
(B) Farming was an established, organized part of Native life in the region shown.
(C) Europeans introduced maize and bean farming to North America in the 1500s.
(D) Native peoples in the region planted crops only after Spanish missions arrived.
items.explanation: The engraving shows Indigenous people planting beans and maize in prepared fields, which is direct visual evidence that agriculture was already an organized practice in eastern North America before sustained European contact. The image was based on drawings made in the 1500s, depicting practices that predated colonization.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the image shows people planting crops, so it contradicts the idea that everyone relied only on hunting.
option_explanations.B: Right — the image documents organized planting of maize and beans, evidence of established Native agriculture.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — maize and beans were Native American crops; Europeans encountered them here, they did not introduce them.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the 1591 engraving depicts practices from before Spanish missions reached this region.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Three Sisters agriculture: the interplanting of maize, beans, and squash that sustained dense Native populations in eastern North America

items.stem: The 'three sisters' system — interplanting maize, beans, and squash in the same field — sustained dense Native populations in eastern North America. Which statement best explains why this system could support large, settled communities?
options: (A) It required iron plows and teams of draft animals to work the soil effectively.
(B) It succeeded only in desert regions where very little rainfall occurred.
(C) It was designed from the start to grow large surplus crops for export to European markets overseas.
(D) It produced three food crops from the same cleared field, increasing each planting's yield.
items.explanation: Growing three complementary food crops together on the same land multiplied what each cleared field could produce. That larger, reliable food supply is what allowed communities to grow dense and stay settled in one place.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — iron plows and draft animals came with Europeans; this was a pre-contact Native system.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the three sisters system supported populations in eastern North America, not the desert Southwest.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the system predated European contact, so it could not have been designed for European markets.
option_explanations.D: Right — three crops from one field meant more food per planting, supporting denser settlement.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Three Sisters agriculture: the interplanting of maize, beans, and squash that sustained dense Native populations in eastern North America

items.stem: The chart compares the approximate populations of two cities built before Europeans arrived in the Americas. Which claim is best supported by this comparison?

stimulus.caption: Approximate populations of two pre-contact American cities at their height.

chart_spec.title: City size before European contact
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures from u1.md §The story: Tenochtitlan a 'lake city of hundreds of thousands'; Cahokia held 'tens of thousands of residents at its height around 1100'

options: (A) Only the societies of Mesoamerica were capable of building large and complex cities anywhere in the Americas.
(B) Cahokia and Tenochtitlan shared the same form of government and social structure.
(C) Maize-based farming could support very large cities in different regions of the Americas.
(D) European cities were always smaller than Native American cities in this period.
items.explanation: Both cities were large — one in the hundreds of thousands, the other in the tens of thousands — and both were supported by intensive maize agriculture, one in central Mexico and one in the North American Midwest. The comparison shows that farming could sustain major urban populations in widely separated regions.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — Cahokia's tens of thousands show large cities also developed north of Mexico.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — similar size does not mean the same government; the chart gives no information about political systems.
option_explanations.C: Right — the two cities, in different regions, both show maize agriculture supporting very large populations.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the chart compares two American cities with each other; it says nothing about European cities.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — the Mexica built Tenochtitlan, 'a lake city of hundreds of thousands'; Cahokia 'held tens of thousands of residents at its height around 1100'

items.stem: This 1771 map (shown in facsimile) marks Cahokia on the Mississippi River, near present-day St. Louis. Mississippian chiefdoms like Cahokia built their towns in the river valleys of the Southeast and Midwest. Which factor best explains this location pattern?

stimulus.image_caption: Facsimile of 'A Plan of the several Villages in the Illinois Country, with Part of the River Mississippi,' by Thomas Hutchins (1771), showing Cahokia on the Mississippi River.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Facsimile of a 1771 map, published in an 1889 book; pre-1930 work

options: (A) River valleys provided fertile floodplain soils for the maize surpluses chiefdoms depended on.
(B) The Mexica Empire, centered far to the south in central Mexico, had already claimed all of the upland areas.
(C) Spanish officials ordered Native towns to be built along rivers for easier control.
(D) Rivers were the only source of drinking water available anywhere in North America.
items.explanation: Mississippian societies were maize-farming chiefdoms, and river floodplains offered the rich, renewable soils that made large maize harvests possible. Those surpluses fed dense populations and supported the chiefs, priests, and builders of places like Cahokia.

option_explanations.A: Right — fertile river-valley soils grew the maize surpluses that sustained chiefdom populations.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the Mexica Empire was in central Mexico, far from the Mississippi Valley.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — these towns and their locations predate Spanish colonization of the region.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — fresh water existed in many places; the key advantage of river valleys was fertile farmland.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — 'Mississippian chiefdoms farmed the river valleys of the Southeast and Midwest — Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, held tens of thousands of residents at its height around 1100'

items.stem: Pueblo peoples farmed in the arid Southwest, Iroquois villagers lived in the woodlands of the Northeast, and the peoples of the Pacific Northwest built their lives around fishing. Taken together, what do these examples best illustrate?
options: (A) Native societies in every environment adopted identical farming methods and crops.
(B) Native societies shaped their economies and ways of life around their environments.
(C) Only maize-farming societies were able to establish permanent settlements anywhere.
(D) Geographic differences kept all Native societies completely isolated from one another.
items.explanation: Each group made a living in a way that fit its environment — dry farming in the Southwest, woodland village farming in the Northeast, fishing on the Northwest coast. The pattern is adaptation: different environments produced different ways of life.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the examples show different adaptations, not identical methods.
option_explanations.B: Right — farming, village life, and fishing each fit a particular environment.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — Pacific Northwest fishing peoples maintained settled communities without maize agriculture.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the review describes different adaptations, not total isolation.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — 'Pueblo farmers in the Southwest, Iroquois villagers in the Northeast, fishing peoples of the Pacific Northwest — had each adapted their way of life to a particular environment'

items.stem: Historians observe that where maize farming supported dense populations, complex hierarchies developed, while societies without intensive farming stayed smaller and more mobile. Which explanation best accounts for this pattern?
options: (A) Farming societies possessed superior weapons that forced neighboring peoples to obey them.
(B) Mobile societies held votes and decided to reject all forms of leadership.
(C) Maize could only be planted by societies that already had kings and priests.
(D) Farming produced food surpluses that fed non-farming specialists like chiefs and priests.
items.explanation: A surplus is the key: when farmers grow more food than their own families need, the extra can support full-time leaders, religious specialists, and craftspeople. That division of labor is what makes complex hierarchies possible.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the pattern is about food production, not weapons.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the review describes smaller, mobile life, not a political decision against leadership.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — this reverses the causation; farming came first and made hierarchy possible.
option_explanations.D: Right — surpluses freed some people from farming, allowing specialized roles and hierarchy.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — 'The single biggest divide among them was agriculture: where maize farming supported dense populations, complex hierarchies followed; where it did not, life stayed smaller and more mobile'

items.stem: A student claims that Native American societies were simple and unchanging before Europeans arrived. Which piece of evidence best challenges this claim?
options: (A) All Native societies across the entire Americas spoke a single common language.
(B) No agriculture existed anywhere in the Americas before the year 1492.
(C) Cahokia's earthen mounds rivaled the largest constructions in Europe.
(D) The Inca Empire had no roads or storehouses.
items.explanation: If a North American society could organize the labor to raise earthworks on the scale of anything in Europe, it was neither simple nor static. Cahokia's mounds are direct evidence of large-scale organization and ambition before contact.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the Americas held hundreds of distinct societies and languages, not one.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — maize farming was widespread and supported dense populations.
option_explanations.C: Right — monumental construction on a European scale contradicts 'simple and unchanging.'
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the Inca did build extensive roads and storehouses.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — Cahokia had 'earthen mounds that rivaled anything in Europe'; u1.md §What the exam tests here — 'Compare Native societies by environment and adaptation... the exam rewards linking social complexity to food production, not listing tribes'

items.stem: The Iroquois lived in settled villages in the Northeast woodlands. Which development best explains how permanent village life was possible there?
options: (A) Three sisters agriculture, which sustained dense populations in eastern North America.
(B) The use of horses to plow large fields and transport heavy harvests.
(C) Year-round hunting of migratory bison herds across the Great Plains.
(D) Tribute payments collected regularly from neighboring empires, as practiced by the Mexica.
items.explanation: Permanent villages need a reliable local food supply. In the eastern woodlands, the three sisters system provided it — three crops grown together that fed dense, settled populations year after year.

option_explanations.A: Right — three sisters farming sustained the dense populations of eastern North America.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — horses arrived with Europeans; Iroquois villages predate them.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — bison hunting was a Plains pattern, not the basis of Northeast woodland villages.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — tribute empires describe the Mexica, not Iroquois villagers.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — 'Iroquois villagers in the Northeast'; u1.md §Key terms — Three Sisters agriculture 'sustained dense Native populations in eastern North America'

items.stem: This 1880 photograph shows Taos Pueblo in New Mexico: multi-story adobe dwellings clustered together in an arid landscape. What does this image best illustrate about Pueblo adaptation to the Southwest?

stimulus.image_caption: Photograph of Taos Pueblo, New Mexico, 1880: multi-story adobe dwellings in an arid landscape.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1880 albumen photograph; pre-1930, public domain (Library of Congress)

options: (A) Pueblo peoples depended on river floodplains exactly like the Mississippians did.
(B) Pueblo peoples built a settled farming society suited to a dry environment.
(C) The Spanish introduced adobe architecture to the Southwest during the 1800s.
(D) Pueblo communities were temporary camps that relocated with each season.
items.explanation: The tightly clustered adobe buildings, made from local earth and suited to a dry climate, show a farming people who adapted their housing and village life to the arid Southwest — a very different answer to farming than the river-valley towns of the Mississippians.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the arid Southwest lacked the great floodplains of the Southeast and Midwest; the adaptation was different.
option_explanations.B: Right — adobe construction and compact villages fit an arid farming environment.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — pueblo adobe architecture is a Native tradition far older than the 1800s.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the substantial multi-story buildings show permanent settlement, not seasonal camps.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — 'Pueblo farmers in the Southwest... had each adapted their way of life to a particular environment'

items.stem: The 1591 engraving below shows Florida Indians hunting deer while disguised under deerskins. An earlier engraving from the same series showed the same people planting beans and maize. What do the two images together best demonstrate?

stimulus.image_caption: Engraving by Theodor de Bry (1591), after Jacques Le Moyne de Morgues, showing Florida Indians hunting deer disguised under deerskins.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1591 engraving; pre-1930, public domain (Library of Congress)

options: (A) Hunting was far more important than farming to every Native society throughout the Americas.
(B) Native peoples combined farming with hunting rather than relying on one food source.
(C) Native peoples gave up farming entirely once they learned to hunt deer.
(D) Only societies without any agriculture ever hunted animals for food.
items.explanation: The same community is shown both planting crops and hunting deer, which means their economy mixed the two. Farming provided staple crops while hunting added meat and other resources — a diversified way of making a living.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the images show both activities, and 'every Native society' overgeneralizes from one region.
option_explanations.B: Right — the pair shows one people both farming and hunting.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the images show both practices existing side by side, not one replacing the other.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — this very example shows a farming people hunting too.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — Native societies 'had each adapted their way of life to a particular environment'; u1.md §What the exam tests here — compare adaptations rather than listing tribes

items.stem: Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, held tens of thousands of residents around 1100 — nearly four centuries before Columbus reached the Americas. What is the most significant implication of this fact?
options: (A) Cahokia was founded by European explorers seeking gold.
(B) Every Native society in North America was as large and as complex as Cahokia was.
(C) Cahokia served as the capital of the Mexica Empire in Mexico.
(D) Large, complex societies arose in North America without any European contact.
items.explanation: Cahokia reached its height around 1100, centuries before any European arrived. Its size proves that urban-scale complexity in North America was a homegrown development, not something introduced from across the Atlantic.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — Cahokia predates European arrival by centuries.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — Cahokia was the largest society north of Mexico; most were smaller.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the Mexica Empire was centered in central Mexico, far to the south.
option_explanations.D: Right — a city of tens of thousands around 1100 shows independent development of complexity.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — 'Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, held tens of thousands of residents at its height around 1100'

items.stem: Raising Cahokia's great earthen mounds meant moving millions of cubic feet of earth by hand, carried basket by basket. Which conclusion about Mississippian society follows most directly from this evidence?
options: (A) Mississippians used wheeled carts pulled by draft animals for their large construction projects.
(B) The mounds were built by enslaved European laborers under Spanish overseers.
(C) Mississippian leaders could organize and direct the labor of thousands of people.
(D) The builders left written records describing their system of government.
items.explanation: Moving that much earth by hand requires feeding, housing, and coordinating huge work crews over many years. Only a society with recognized authority and organization could pull that off — so the mounds themselves are evidence of centralized leadership.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — no wheeled carts or draft animals existed in pre-contact North America.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the mounds were raised centuries before Europeans arrived.
option_explanations.C: Right — massive hand-built earthworks imply leaders who could mobilize large labor forces.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the mounds are archaeological evidence; they do not include written records.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — Cahokia's 'earthen mounds that rivaled anything in Europe'; complex hierarchies followed where maize farming supported dense populations

items.stem: Which pairing correctly matches a Native American group with its environmental adaptation before European contact?
options: (A) Pacific Northwest peoples — maize farming in inland river valleys
(B) Mississippian peoples — deep-sea fishing along the Pacific coast
(C) Pueblo peoples — farming adapted to the arid Southwest
(D) Iroquois villagers — bison hunting on the Great Plains
items.explanation: Each group adapted to its own environment: Pueblo farmers to the arid Southwest, Mississippians to southeastern and midwestern river valleys, Iroquois villagers to the Northeast woodlands, and Pacific Northwest peoples to coastal fishing.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — Pacific Northwest peoples built their lives around fishing, not inland maize farming.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — Mississippians farmed river valleys in the Southeast and Midwest, not the Pacific coast.
option_explanations.C: Right — Pueblo farmers adapted agriculture to the arid Southwest.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the Iroquois were woodland villagers, not Plains bison hunters.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — 'Mississippian chiefdoms farmed the river valleys of the Southeast and Midwest'; 'Pueblo farmers in the Southwest, Iroquois villagers in the Northeast, fishing peoples of the Pacific Northwest'

items.stem: A historian argues that food production — more than any other factor — determined how complex a Native American society became. Which comparison would provide the strongest test of this argument?
options: (A) Comparing a maize-farming chiefdom with a non-farming foraging society in the same environment.
(B) Comparing two maize-farming societies located in very different regions.
(C) Comparing the religious ceremonies and rituals of the Mexica of Mexico and the Inca of the Andes.
(D) Comparing European metal tools with the stone tools used by Native peoples.
items.explanation: To test whether food production is the decisive factor, you need to hold other things constant and vary only food production. Comparing farmers with non-farmers in a similar environment isolates food production as the variable being tested.

option_explanations.A: Right — same environment, different food production: the comparison isolates the factor in question.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — both societies farm, so the comparison cannot test whether farming itself is decisive.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — religion is a different variable from food production.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — tools are not the factor the argument is about.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — 'The single biggest divide among them was agriculture: where maize farming supported dense populations, complex hierarchies followed; where it did not, life stayed smaller and more mobile'

items.stem: The review notes that Cahokia's earthen mounds 'rivaled anything in Europe.' Why do historians emphasize this comparison?
options: (A) To prove that European visitors learned their mound-building techniques directly from Cahokia.
(B) To show that Cahokia was actually a European colony in disguise.
(C) To argue that all Native societies everywhere built mounds identical to those at Cahokia.
(D) To show that monumental building was achieved in the Americas without Old World contact.
items.explanation: The comparison is about independent achievement: a North American society raised earthworks on the scale of Europe's greatest buildings without any contact with Europe. It corrects the assumption that only Old World civilizations built on a monumental scale.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — there was no contact, so no learning in either direction.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — Cahokia was a Native city centuries before Europeans arrived.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — mound-building varied; the point is the scale of Cahokia's achievement.
option_explanations.D: Right — the comparison highlights independent American achievement in monumental building.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — Cahokia's 'earthen mounds that rivaled anything in Europe'

items.stem: In the three sisters system, tall maize stalks rise above climbing bean vines while broad squash leaves spread across the ground below. This arrangement best illustrates which feature of Native American agriculture?
options: (A) Planting a single crop across enormous cleared fields to maximize the harvest yield.
(B) Combining crops so that each uses a different layer of the growing space.
(C) Leaving fields unplanted for years at a time to rest the soil.
(D) Clearing forests with European iron axes and saws.
items.explanation: The three plants occupy different layers — maize grows tall, beans climb the stalks, squash covers the ground. Stacking crops this way squeezes more food out of every cleared field, which is the core logic of interplanting.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — that describes monoculture, the opposite of interplanting.
option_explanations.B: Right — three crops share one field by using different layers of space.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the system is about planting together, not leaving land idle.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — this was a pre-contact Native system, developed without European tools.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Three Sisters agriculture: 'the interplanting of maize, beans, and squash that sustained dense Native populations in eastern North America'

items.stem: The 1591 de Bry engravings of Native farming and hunting were made by a European artist who never visited North America, working from watercolors painted by an English colonist. What is the most important limitation of these engravings as historical evidence?
options: (A) They prove that every Native society farmed in exactly the same way.
(B) They were created long after all Native societies in the region had completely disappeared.
(C) They show Native life through European eyes and may reflect European assumptions.
(D) They contain no information that historians can reliably use.
items.explanation: De Bry never saw the people he engraved; he reworked a colonist's watercolors for a European audience. Details like poses, clothing, and settings may have been adjusted to match what Europeans expected, so historians must read these images critically rather than as direct records.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — two engravings of one region cannot prove uniformity across a continent.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the engravings date to 1591, when these societies were very much alive.
option_explanations.C: Right — a European artist who never visited is a mediated, possibly distorted source.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — used carefully, the engravings still document real practices like planting and hunting.

items.fact_source: Stimulus metadata (Wikimedia Commons) — engraved by Theodor de Bry (1528–1598) after Jacques Le Moyne de Morgues; u1.md §What the exam tests here — European accounts are sourcing material to be read critically for perspective and purpose

items.stem: Which statement best summarizes the relationship between environment and social organization among Native American societies before 1492?
options: (A) Farming regions could support dense, hierarchical societies; other regions supported smaller, more mobile ones.
(B) Societies living in similar environments always developed identical cultures, institutions, and political systems without exception.
(C) Native societies succeeded by ignoring the limits imposed by their environments.
(D) Only societies located on ocean coasts ever developed any form of social organization.
items.explanation: The review's central point is that food production — made possible or limited by the environment — shaped everything else. Rich farmland meant surpluses, dense populations, and hierarchy; elsewhere, life stayed smaller and mobile. Environment set the range of what was possible.

option_explanations.A: Right — this restates the review's core argument about agriculture and complexity.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — 'always identical' is far too absolute; adaptation varied.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the pattern is precisely that societies worked within environmental possibilities.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — Cahokia and other inland farming societies were highly organized.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — 'The single biggest divide among them was agriculture: where maize farming supported dense populations, complex hierarchies followed; where it did not, life stayed smaller and more mobile'

items.stem: Archaeologists have mapped Cahokia's mounds, plazas, and defensive palisade. Which question about Cahokia can this kind of archaeological evidence answer most reliably?
options: (A) What the residents called their city and what language its people spoke.
(B) Exactly how many people lived in Cahokia during each year of its long history.
(C) What the residents believed about the afterlife and spiritual world.
(D) Whether the society could organize and sustain large-scale construction.
items.explanation: Mounds, plazas, and walls are physical facts: someone planned them, fed the workers, and kept the project going. That directly answers whether the society could organize large-scale construction. Names, exact yearly censuses, and beliefs about the afterlife leave no direct trace in earthworks.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — earthworks cannot reveal what people called their city or what language they spoke.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — archaeology gives population estimates, not exact yearly counts.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — beliefs are difficult to recover reliably from mounds and plazas alone.
option_explanations.D: Right — monumental construction is direct evidence of organizational capacity.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — Cahokia's 'earthen mounds that rivaled anything in Europe'; complex hierarchies where maize farming supported dense populations

items.stem: The review describes a basic divide: where maize farming supported dense populations, life was settled and hierarchical; where it did not, life 'stayed smaller and more mobile.' Which group best represents the 'smaller and more mobile' side of this divide?
options: (A) The Mexica of the great lake city of Tenochtitlan in central Mexico.
(B) Foraging bands in regions without maize agriculture.
(C) The Inca of the Andean highlands.
(D) The chiefdoms of the Mississippian culture.
items.explanation: The divide is about food production. The Mexica, Inca, and Mississippians all practiced intensive agriculture and built dense, hierarchical societies. Foraging bands — living where farming was not practiced — stayed smaller and mobile, exactly the other side of the divide.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — Tenochtitlan held hundreds of thousands; the settled, hierarchical side.
option_explanations.B: Right — non-farming foragers match the 'smaller and more mobile' description.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the Inca ran a vast, organized empire.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — Mississippian chiefdoms were settled and hierarchical.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — 'where maize farming supported dense populations, complex hierarchies followed; where it did not, life stayed smaller and more mobile'

items.stem: Under the encomienda system, the Spanish Crown granted a colonist the right to demand labor and tribute from a Native community. In theory, what did the colonist owe the community in return?
options: (A) Christian instruction for the Native community.
(B) Full legal ownership of the community's farmland and water rights.
(C) A share of the silver mined at Potosí.
(D) Military protection against French colonists.
items.explanation: The encomienda was framed as an exchange: the colonist received Native labor and tribute, and in return was supposed to provide Christian teaching and protection. In practice the labor demands overwhelmed any instruction, but instruction was the official justification.

option_explanations.A: Right — Christian instruction was the theoretical justification for the grant.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the encomienda granted labor and tribute, not land ownership.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — Potosí silver flowed to the Crown and the world economy, not to Native communities.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — defense against the French was not part of the encomienda's terms.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Encomienda: 'Spanish grant giving a colonist the right to extract labor and tribute from Native communities, in theory in exchange for Christian instruction'

items.stem: Las Casas wrote the passage below to persuade the Spanish Crown to reform its colonial policies. How does that purpose shape the passage?

stimulus.text: Now the ultimate end and scope that incited the Spaniards to endeavor the Extirptaion and Desolation of this People, was Gold only; that thereby growing opulent in a short time, they might arrive at once at such Degrees and Dignities, as were no wayes consistent with their Persons. Finally, in one word, their Ambition and Avarice, than which the heart of Man never entertained greater...
stimulus.attribution: Bartolomé de las Casas, A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (originally published in Seville, 1552; this English translation, 1689). Text verbatim from Project Gutenberg EBook #20321 (italic markers removed).

options: (A) He praises the encomienda system as fundamentally fair and just.
(B) He argues that Native peoples possessed no rights whatsoever under Spain.
(C) He stresses Spanish greed and cruelty to make reform seem urgent.
(D) He avoids blaming any Spaniards so the Crown will not take offense.
items.explanation: Las Casas was writing as an advocate, not a neutral observer. By painting the colonists' motives as pure gold-lust and describing the results as 'extirpation,' he aimed to shock the Crown into action. Recognizing that purpose helps readers understand why the passage emphasizes the worst abuses.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the passage condemns the colonists' conduct; it does not praise the encomienda.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — Las Casas spent his career arguing that Native peoples did possess natural rights.
option_explanations.C: Right — an advocate for reform highlights the evils that reform must address.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the passage directly blames Spanish 'Ambition and Avarice.'

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Bartolomé de las Casas: 'the Dominican friar whose writings denounced Spanish cruelty and helped curb (but not end) Native enslavement'; u1.md §What the exam tests here — 'Las Casas and the Valladolid debate are perfect sourcing material'

items.stem: The New Laws of 1542, pushed by Bartolomé de las Casas, did which of the following?
options: (A) Abolished all forced labor in the Spanish Empire immediately.
(B) Gave Native leaders voting seats in the Spanish government.
(C) Transferred the encomienda from individual colonists to the Catholic Church.
(D) Limited the encomienda and forbade new grants of Native labor.
items.explanation: The New Laws were a reform, not an abolition. They restricted the encomienda system — limiting existing grants and banning new ones — which is why they count as a curb on the system rather than its end.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the laws limited the encomienda; they did not abolish all forced labor.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — nothing in the New Laws created Native representation in Spanish government.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the laws restricted grants; they did not hand the system to the Church.
option_explanations.D: Right — limiting the encomienda and forbidding new grants is exactly what the New Laws did.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — New Laws (1542): 'Spanish reforms, pushed by Las Casas, that limited the encomienda and forbade new grants of Native labor'

items.stem: After the New Laws limited the encomienda, Spain increasingly imported enslaved Africans under the asiento system. Which statement best describes what changed and what stayed the same in Spanish colonial labor?
options: (A) Forced labor ended and was replaced everywhere by free wage labor.
(B) Coerced labor continued, but shifted from Native peoples to enslaved Africans.
(C) The encomienda expanded because the New Laws were never enforced anywhere in the colonies.
(D) Spain abandoned its American colonies entirely for lack of workers.
items.explanation: This is a continuity-and-change pattern: the demand for coerced workers never went away, so the system adapted. What changed was who was forced to work — as Native labor became harder to exploit, enslaved Africans were imported to take their place.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — coerced labor did not end; it changed form.
option_explanations.B: Right — the coercion continued while its victims changed.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the New Laws did limit the encomienda; the shift to African slavery is the evidence.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — Spain kept its empire; it replaced the labor force rather than leaving.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — 'Spain kept the empire but began replacing Native forced labor with enslaved Africans, imported under the asiento system — a fateful shift'; u1.md §What the exam tests here — 'Labor systems over time — from encomienda to the New Laws to African slavery: coerced labor continues, but who is coerced changes'

items.stem: At Valladolid in 1550–1551, Las Casas debated Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda over whether Native peoples possessed natural rights and rational humanity. What is the historical significance of this debate?
options: (A) It shows the morality of conquest was openly contested in 1500s Spain.
(B) It immediately ended the encomienda system throughout the empire.
(C) It demonstrated that all Spaniards agreed the conquest was fully justified.
(D) It convinced Spain to abandon its American colonies for good.
items.explanation: The debate matters because it happened at all: at the height of Spain's empire, the Crown sponsored a formal argument about whether its conquests were just. That tells us conquest was controversial even among the conquerors — it was contested in its own time, not only by later historians.

option_explanations.A: Right — a formal Crown-sponsored debate proves the morality of empire was disputed in the 1500s.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the encomienda had already been limited by the New Laws, and the debate did not end it.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the debate's existence proves disagreement, not agreement.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — Spain kept its empire for centuries after Valladolid.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Valladolid Debate (1550–1551): 'the formal dispute between Las Casas and Sepulveda over the rights and rational humanity of Native peoples'; u1.md §What the exam tests here — 'Conquest was contested at the time'

items.stem: In the passage below, Las Casas identifies which motive as the driving force behind the destruction of Native peoples?

stimulus.text: Finally, in one word, their Ambition and Avarice, than which the heart of Man never entertained greater, and the vast Wealth of those Regions; the Humility and Patience of the Inhabitants (which made their approach to these Lands more facil and easie) did much promote the business: Whom they so despicably contemned, that they treated them (I speak of things which I was an Eye Witness of, without the least fallacy) not as Beasts, which I cordially wished they would, but as the most abject dung and filth of the Earth...
stimulus.attribution: Bartolomé de las Casas, A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (originally published in Seville, 1552; this English translation, 1689). Text verbatim from Project Gutenberg EBook #20321.

options: (A) A sincere desire to spread Christianity.
(B) Direct orders from the Spanish king to destroy Native communities.
(C) Self-defense against repeated Native attacks.
(D) Gold, and the ambition and greed for quick wealth and status.
items.explanation: Las Casas is explicit: 'the ultimate end... was Gold only,' pursued through 'Ambition and Avarice.' He argues the colonists wanted fast riches and the social rank that came with them, and treated Native peoples as obstacles to that wealth.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — Las Casas says the motive was gold and greed, not missionary zeal.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — he blames the colonists' avarice, not royal orders; the Crown later passed the reforming New Laws.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — he insists the Spaniards 'never received any injury from the Indians.'
option_explanations.D: Right — gold, ambition, and avarice are the motives he names.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Bartolomé de las Casas: 'writings denounced Spanish cruelty'

items.stem: This 18th-century casta painting is labeled 'De español e india, mestiza' — 'From a Spaniard and an Indigenous woman, a mestiza child.' What does this painting best illustrate about Spanish colonial society?

stimulus.image_caption: Casta painting labeled 'De español e india, mestiza' (From a Spaniard and an Indigenous woman, a mestiza child), 18th century.

options: (A) Spaniards and Native peoples never mixed or formed families with each other in the colonies.
(B) Colonial artists refused to depict mixed-ancestry families in their work.
(C) The colonial regime carefully classified people according to their ancestry.
(D) The casta system treated every child identically regardless of parentage.
items.explanation: Casta paintings exist because colonial society was organized around ancestry: each combination of parents produced a named category with legal and social consequences. Painting and labeling a 'mestiza' child shows how seriously the regime took classifying people by descent.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the painting itself depicts a mixed family, so mixing clearly occurred.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — casta paintings are precisely depictions of mixed families.
option_explanations.C: Right — the labeled categories show ancestry-based classification.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the whole point of the casta system was to treat people differently by ancestry.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — 'Mestizaje and the casta system — racial mixing in Spanish America and the elaborate legal hierarchy that ranked people by ancestry'

items.stem: This 18th-century casta painting is labeled 'De negra y español sale mulato' — 'From a Black woman and a Spaniard comes a mulatto child.' What does this label reveal about the casta system?

stimulus.image_caption: Anonymous 18th-century casta painting labeled 'De negra y español sale mulato' (From a Black woman and a Spaniard comes a mulatto child).

options: (A) The system classified only people of Spanish and Indigenous ancestry.
(B) The system also classified the children of enslaved Africans, assigning them a named place.
(C) The system abolished slavery for all children of mixed ancestry.
(D) Spanish law prohibited any classification of African-descended people anywhere in the colonies.
items.explanation: The casta system covered everyone in the colonies, including the growing population of African descent. A 'mulato' label shows that children of African and Spanish parents were also sorted into the ancestry hierarchy — the system's reach extended to the enslaved population and their descendants.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — this painting classifies African-Spanish parentage, not Indigenous.
option_explanations.B: Right — the mulato category shows the hierarchy included people of African descent.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — classification did not abolish slavery or change anyone's legal bondage.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the painting itself is a classification of an African-descended child.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — 'Mestizaje and the casta system — racial mixing in Spanish America and the elaborate legal hierarchy that ranked people by ancestry'

items.stem: This casta painting labels the child 'cambujo,' the offspring of a mulatto father and a 'china' (mixed-ancestry) mother — one of dozens of such precise labels. The existence of so many specific categories is best understood as evidence of which colonial concern?

stimulus.image_caption: Anonymous 18th-century casta painting labeled 'De mulato y china sale cambujo' (From a mulatto and a china comes a cambujo child).

options: (A) The drive to fix each person's legal and social status by ancestry, even as mixing continued.
(B) A scientific program to study human biology and heredity in the colonies, sponsored by the Crown.
(C) Proof that colonial racial categories were stable, fixed, and never changed over time.
(D) An official campaign to eliminate all racial distinctions in colonial society.
items.explanation: The labels multiplied because reality kept outrunning them: people continued to mix, so the system kept inventing new names to pin everyone down. Dozens of categories show a regime anxious to classify a population that would not stay within neat boundaries.

option_explanations.A: Right — ever-finer labels show the effort to fix status by ancestry amid ongoing mixing.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the categories served legal and social hierarchy, not science.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — multiplying categories show the system straining, not standing still.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the paintings created distinctions; they did not eliminate them.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — 'the elaborate legal hierarchy that ranked people by ancestry'

items.stem: The asiento system is best described as which of the following?
options: (A) The famous 1494 treaty that divided the entire non-European world between Spain and Portugal.
(B) The Spanish Crown's monopoly contract for supplying enslaved Africans to Spanish America.
(C) A religious vow taken by missionaries serving in New Mexico.
(D) A system of elected town councils governing the Spanish colonies.
items.explanation: As Spain shifted from Native to African forced labor, it needed a steady supply of enslaved people. The asiento was the Crown's solution: a monopoly contract granting one party the exclusive right to ship enslaved Africans to Spanish America.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the division of the Americas was the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494).
option_explanations.B: Right — the asiento was the monopoly contract for the African slave supply.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — missionaries took vows, but 'asiento' was a commercial monopoly, not a vow.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — town councils (cabildos) were a different institution entirely.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Asiento system: 'the Spanish monopoly contract for supplying enslaved Africans to the Americas'

items.stem: The great silver mines at Potosí began producing in 1545, and their output flowed into European treasuries and the world economy. What was the significance of Potosí silver for the Spanish Empire?
options: (A) It ended Spain's need for any colonial labor in the mines or on plantations.
(B) It financed Spanish state power and tied the Americas to the global economy.
(C) It was used only to decorate colonial churches.
(D) It convinced Spain to abandon silver mining entirely and rely on farming instead.
items.explanation: Potosí's silver was the financial engine of Spain's empire: it paid for armies, administration, and the Crown's European ambitions, while drawing the Americas into worldwide trade networks. That is why the mines also demanded so much forced labor.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the mines intensified the demand for labor; they did not end it.
option_explanations.B: Right — silver funded the Spanish state and connected America to the world economy.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — church decoration was trivial next to the fiscal and global significance.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — Spain expanded mining; it did not abandon it.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — 'Spain then built an empire on forced labor — the encomienda system — and on silver, above all the great mines at Potosi (1545), whose output flowed into European treasuries and the world economy'

items.stem: Epidemic disease killed enormous numbers of Native people who had no immunity to European illnesses. Which statement best explains how this demographic catastrophe reshaped Spanish colonial labor?
options: (A) It proved that Native peoples were biologically unsuited to agricultural work of any kind.
(B) It led Spain to free all enslaved workers throughout the colonies.
(C) It had no significant effect on how colonial labor was organized or supplied.
(D) It created a labor shortage that pushed Spain to import enslaved Africans.
items.explanation: The encomienda depended on Native workers, and disease destroyed that workforce. With Native labor collapsing — and Las Casas's reforms making it harder to exploit — Spain turned to a new source of coerced workers: enslaved Africans brought in under the asiento monopoly.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the deaths were caused by lack of immunity to disease, not by unsuitability for work.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — Spain expanded coerced labor; it did not free workers.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the labor shortage was one of the catastrophe's largest consequences.
option_explanations.D: Right — dying Native populations created the shortage that African slavery filled.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — epidemic disease 'killed enormous numbers of Native people who had no immunity'; 'Spain kept the empire but began replacing Native forced labor with enslaved Africans, imported under the asiento system'

items.stem: Historians rely on Las Casas's writings as evidence of Spanish cruelty, but they also know he wrote to persuade the Crown to reform. Which statement best reflects how historians should use his account?
options: (A) It is a Spanish critic's view of the conquest, but its claims must be weighed against his reformist purpose.
(B) It is useless as historical evidence because Las Casas never actually visited the Americas himself.
(C) It should be accepted uncritically because its author was a Catholic priest.
(D) It proves that every single Spaniard living anywhere in the Americas actively and openly opposed the encomienda system.
items.explanation: Good historical practice treats Las Casas as what he was: an eyewitness with an agenda. His account preserves real descriptions of cruelty, but his goal — moving the Crown to act — means historians check his claims against other evidence rather than taking every detail at face value.

option_explanations.A: Right — use the account while accounting for the author's purpose.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — Las Casas lived in the Americas for decades; and a persuasive purpose does not make a source useless.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — no source is accepted uncritically, regardless of the author's occupation.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — one critic's account cannot prove what every Spaniard thought.

items.fact_source: u1.md §What the exam tests here — 'Las Casas and the Valladolid debate are perfect sourcing material: even in the 1500s, Europeans argued about the morality of empire'

items.stem: The Pueblo Revolt of 1680 is best described as which of the following?
options: (A) A Spanish military campaign that conquered the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico.
(B) A peaceful negotiation that gave Pueblo leaders permanent seats in the Spanish colonial government.
(C) A coordinated Native uprising under Popé that drove the Spanish from New Mexico for over a decade.
(D) A revolt by Spanish settlers against the Crown's tax policies in New Mexico.
items.explanation: In 1680, Pueblo communities across New Mexico rose together under Popé's leadership, killing colonists and missionaries and driving the Spanish out entirely. Spain did not reestablish control for more than a decade — one of the most successful Native resistances in colonial North America.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the revolt was Native peoples rising against the Spanish, not the reverse.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — it was a violent uprising and expulsion, not a negotiation.
option_explanations.C: Right — coordinated, led by Popé, and it removed the Spanish for over a decade.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the rebels were Pueblo Native peoples, not Spanish settlers.

items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms — Pueblo Revolt (1680): 'the coordinated Native uprising under Pope that expelled Spanish colonists and missionaries from New Mexico'

items.stem: Spain had held New Mexico since 1610 through its mission system. Which factor best explains why the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 succeeded in expelling the Spanish entirely instead of being quickly suppressed?
options: (A) The Spanish voluntarily withdrew to concentrate on defending Florida.
(B) French armies invaded New Mexico and defeated the Spanish garrisons there.
(C) Pueblo communities across many villages coordinated under Popé, striking simultaneously.
(D) A European epidemic wiped out the Spanish missionaries in New Mexico before the fighting even began.
items.explanation: The review stresses that the revolt was 'coordinated': Popé organized villages across New Mexico to rise at the same time. Simultaneous attacks left the Spanish unable to concentrate their forces or relieve the missions one by one — coordination turned scattered grievances into an expulsion.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the Spanish were driven out; they did not choose to leave.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — no French army invaded New Mexico in 1680.
option_explanations.C: Right — coordination across villages is what made the revolt succeed.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — epidemic disease devastated Native populations; it did not wipe out the missionaries.

items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms — Pueblo Revolt (1680): 'the coordinated Native uprising under Pope that expelled Spanish colonists and missionaries from New Mexico'; u2.md §The story — 'Spain held Florida (St. Augustine, 1565) and New Mexico (Santa Fe, 1610) through missions'

items.stem: The Pueblo Revolt is often studied alongside other acts of resistance in the colonial period. As an example of Native resistance to Spanish colonization, the revolt best illustrates which broader pattern?
options: (A) Long-term cooperation between Native peoples and Spanish missionaries throughout New Mexico.
(B) A dispute between rival Spanish colonial governors over authority.
(C) An English-backed plot to seize control of New Mexico.
(D) Sustained Native opposition to coerced labor and mission control in the Spanish colonies.
items.explanation: The revolt was not an isolated outburst. Across the Spanish colonies, Native peoples resisted forced labor, tribute, and mission discipline — sometimes by fleeing, sometimes by rebelling. The Pueblo Revolt is the largest and most successful example of that constant resistance.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the rebels killed missionaries and destroyed churches; this was opposition, not cooperation.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the conflict was between Pueblo peoples and the Spanish, not among Spaniards.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — there is no evidence of English involvement; it was a Pueblo-led uprising.
option_explanations.D: Right — the revolt exemplifies the continuous Native resistance to Spanish coercion.

items.fact_source: u2.md §What the exam tests here — 'Resistance from below — Stono, the Pueblo Revolt, and slave codes as cause-and-effect pairs: repression and resistance escalating together'

items.stem: The encomienda was officially justified as an exchange — Native labor and tribute for Christian instruction. Given Las Casas's campaign, the New Laws of 1542, and the eventual shift to enslaved African labor, what does the system's history suggest about that justification?
options: (A) The religious justification covered forced labor that even many Spaniards found indefensible.
(B) The system operated exactly as its defenders described it in their official reports to the Crown.
(C) Native peoples preferred the encomienda to their pre-contact ways of life.
(D) The Catholic Church officially opposed all missionary activity in the colonies.
items.explanation: If the encomienda had truly been a fair exchange of labor for teaching, it would not have produced a crusading critic, reforming laws, and a wholesale switch to a different coerced workforce. The controversy the system generated shows the religious rationale was a cover for exploitation — one that troubled even Spain itself.

option_explanations.A: Right — the protests and reforms reveal the justification as a cover for forced labor.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the campaigns and laws against it prove it did not work as advertised.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — nothing in the record suggests Native peoples preferred it; they resisted it.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the Church ran the missions; it did not oppose missionary activity.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Encomienda: 'in theory in exchange for Christian instruction'; New Laws 'pushed by Las Casas'; u1.md §What the exam tests here — 'from encomienda to the New Laws to African slavery'

items.stem: The New Laws of 1542 limited the encomienda but did not end forced Native labor, and Spain soon expanded African slavery instead. What does this outcome best illustrate?
options: (A) That Spanish reformers had no real influence on colonial policy at all.
(B) That the New Laws actually strengthened and expanded the encomienda system.
(C) That dependence on coerced labor outlasted any single reform of the system.
(D) That Native peoples throughout the colonies were fully liberated by the New Laws.
items.explanation: Reform could change the rules, but it could not change the underlying demand: the colonial economy ran on coerced workers. When one source of forced labor was restricted, the system found another — enslaved Africans. The dependence on coercion survived the reform aimed at it.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — Las Casas's campaign did produce the New Laws; reformers had real influence.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the laws limited the encomienda; they did not expand it.
option_explanations.C: Right — the shift to African slavery shows coerced labor itself continued.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — forced Native labor continued; the laws curbed the system but did not end it.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Las Casas's writings 'helped curb (but not end) Native enslavement'; u1.md §What the exam tests here — 'coerced labor continues, but who is coerced changes'

items.stem: In this 18th-century casta painting, the child's label reads 'torna atrás' — 'return backwards.' What does this label reveal about the concerns of Spanish colonial society?

stimulus.image_caption: Casta painting labeled 'De español y albina, torna atrás' (From a Spaniard and an albina, a 'return backwards' child), 18th century.

options: (A) That colonial society welcomed racial mixing without any reservation.
(B) That colonial elites feared mixing could reverse a family's whiteness and status.
(C) That casta labels were assigned randomly with no social meaning at all.
(D) That Spanish law strictly forbade Spaniards from forming families with non-Spaniards.
items.explanation: 'Return backwards' treats whiteness as something that can be lost: a child of mixed ancestry is labeled as a step back toward a lower status. The label exposes the anxiety underneath the whole system — that the boundaries of the hierarchy were fragile and needed constant policing.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — a label meaning 'return backwards' shows anxiety about mixing, not acceptance.
option_explanations.B: Right — the label expresses fear that mixing reverses whiteness and status.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the labels were deliberate markers of social rank, not random.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — mixed families obviously existed; the paintings depict them.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — 'the elaborate legal hierarchy that ranked people by ancestry'

items.stem: This single canvas gathers sixteen casta paintings, each labeling a different combination of parents and child. What does the existence of such a comprehensive set best indicate about Spanish colonial culture?

stimulus.image_caption: Casta painting containing a complete set of 16 casta combinations (racial classifications in the Spanish colonies), 18th century, oil on canvas.

options: (A) That classifying people by ancestry had become a systematic preoccupation.
(B) That every colonial household in the Americas owned exactly sixteen casta paintings.
(C) That the Spanish Crown had abolished all racial categories entirely.
(D) That casta paintings served as official legal documents in colonial court cases.
items.explanation: A sixteen-panel catalog of ancestry combinations is not casual decoration — it is a system laid out for display. Producing such a complete visual taxonomy shows how deeply the ranking of people by descent had penetrated colonial culture.

option_explanations.A: Right — a sixteen-category visual catalog shows classification as a cultural obsession.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the number sixteen reflects the categories, not household ownership.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the set displays categories; it did not abolish them.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — these were cultural objects displaying the hierarchy, not court records.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — 'Mestizaje and the casta system — racial mixing in Spanish America and the elaborate legal hierarchy that ranked people by ancestry'

items.stem: The 'triangular trade' of the 1600s and 1700s is best described as which of the following?
options: (A) A treaty among England, France, and Spain dividing Atlantic trade routes.
(B) Trade conducted only between the three largest English colonies in America.
(C) A system in which each colony traded only with England and no one else.
(D) Three-way Atlantic commerce linking Europe, Africa, and the Americas.
items.explanation: The name describes the shape of the commerce: European goods to Africa, enslaved Africans to the Americas, and American plantation products back to Europe — three legs connecting three continents.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — it was a pattern of commerce, not a diplomatic treaty.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the three points were continents, not three English colonies.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — that describes a misreading of the Navigation Acts, not the triangular trade.
option_explanations.D: Right — Europe, Africa, and the Americas linked by goods, enslaved people, and plantation products.

items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms — Triangular trade: 'the three-way Atlantic commerce linking Europe, Africa, and the Americas in goods, enslaved people, and plantation products'

items.stem: This 1740 English chart of the Atlantic Ocean carefully maps the trade winds and 'the course of sailing from one continent to the other.' What does the chart's focus on winds and sailing courses reveal about transatlantic commerce?

stimulus.image_caption: Emanuel Bowen, 'A new chart of the vast Atlantic Ocean,' 1740, showing the trade winds and the course of sailing from one continent to the other.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1740 chart; pre-1930 with explicit CC0 dedication

options: (A) That merchants depended on predictable wind patterns to move ships.
(B) That steamships had replaced sailing vessels by the year 1740.
(C) That England had little interest in Atlantic trade at the time.
(D) That the chart was designed to discourage merchants from attempting dangerous ocean voyages.
items.explanation: In the age of sail, winds were infrastructure: the trade winds determined which routes ships could take and how long voyages lasted. A chart mapping winds and sailing courses was a practical tool for the merchants whose business depended on them.

option_explanations.A: Right — wind patterns were the basis of sailing routes.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — ocean-going steamships came in the 19th century, not by 1740.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — an English chart of Atlantic sailing courses shows deep English engagement with the trade.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the chart guided voyages; it did not discourage them.

items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms — Triangular trade: 'three-way Atlantic commerce linking Europe, Africa, and the Americas'; the chart documents the sailing routes that commerce used

items.stem: This 1788 diagram shows, deck by deck, exactly how many enslaved people could be packed into the slave ship Brookes 'under the regulated slave trade act of 1788.' What does the diagram's precise measurement of human beings as cargo best demonstrate about the Middle Passage?

stimulus.image_caption: 'Stowage of the British slave ship Brookes under the regulated slave trade act of 1788,' showing the number of enslaved people packed into each deck.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1788 diagram; pre-1930, public domain (Library of Congress)

options: (A) That the 1788 act gave enslaved people comfortable and spacious quarters below deck.
(B) That most Africans crossed the Atlantic as free, paying passengers.
(C) That the slave trade treated enslaved people as cargo packed for maximum profit.
(D) That slave ships carried manufactured goods rather than human beings.
items.explanation: Every figure in the diagram is measured like freight — bodies allocated by the inch to maximize the number carried. Even under a 'regulated' trade, the logic on display is commercial: human beings reduced to cargo space, packed as tightly as the law allowed.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the diagram shows extreme crowding, not comfort.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the people shown were enslaved captives, not free passengers.
option_explanations.C: Right — precise measurement of bodies as cargo shows the trade's commercial dehumanization.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the diagram explicitly shows people, not goods.

items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms — Middle Passage: 'the brutal Atlantic crossing of the transatlantic slave trade, with horrific mortality'

items.stem: Olaudah Equiano, who survived the Middle Passage as a child and published his memoir in 1789, wrote the passage below. Which condition of the Middle Passage does this account most directly document?

stimulus.text: I was soon put down under the decks, and there I received such a salutation in my nostrils as I had never experienced in my life: so that, with the loathsomeness of the stench, and crying together, I became so sick and low that I was not able to eat, nor had I the least desire to taste any thing. I now wished for the last friend, death, to relieve me...
stimulus.attribution: Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano (1789). Text verbatim from Project Gutenberg EBook #15399.

options: (A) The generous and humane treatment of captives by the ship's crew.
(B) A quick and comfortable ocean crossing to the Americas.
(C) The overcrowded, filthy, and despairing conditions below deck.
(D) The willingness of most captives to accept their situation without resistance.
items.explanation: Equiano describes the stench below deck, sickness so severe he could not eat, and despair so deep he wished for death. It is firsthand testimony to the physical and psychological torment of the crossing — exactly the brutal passage the review describes.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — elsewhere he describes being flogged for refusing food, not generous treatment.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — nothing in the passage suggests speed or comfort.
option_explanations.C: Right — stench, sickness, and despair below deck are the passage's direct subjects.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — wishing for death is the opposite of acceptance.

items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms — Middle Passage: 'the brutal Atlantic crossing of the transatlantic slave trade, with horrific mortality'

items.stem: This 1732 engraving shows canoes at Elmina, on the African coast, carrying enslaved people out to European ships anchored offshore. This scene represents which leg of the triangular trade?

stimulus.image_caption: 'Fishing canoes at Elmina and slaves going on board ship at Manfroe,' engraving, 1732: canoes carrying enslaved people out to European ships.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1732 engraving (Jan Kip / Churchill collection); pre-1930, public domain

options: (A) The leg from Africa to the Americas, carrying enslaved people to plantations.
(B) The leg from Europe to Africa, carrying manufactured goods to trade for captives.
(C) The leg from the Americas to Europe, carrying sugar and tobacco.
(D) A voyage unrelated to the triangular trade system of the era.
items.explanation: The engraving captures the embarkation point: enslaved Africans being loaded onto ships bound across the Atlantic. That is the middle leg of the triangle — Africa to the Americas — the Middle Passage itself.

option_explanations.A: Right — enslaved people boarded at African coastal forts for the crossing to the Americas.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the Europe-to-Africa leg carried goods to trade, not enslaved people outward.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the Americas-to-Europe leg carried plantation products, not people from Africa.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the scene shows the slave trade's African embarkation, central to the system.

items.stem: Mercantilism, the dominant economic doctrine of the colonial era, held which of the following?
options: (A) That colonies should trade freely with all nations of the world without restrictions.
(B) That a nation's wealth came only from farming and agriculture.
(C) That governments should not interfere with trade in any way.
(D) That colonies existed to enrich the mother country through favorable trade balances.
items.explanation: Mercantilists measured national power in gold and silver, and saw colonies as instruments for accumulating it: colonial trade should produce a surplus — more exports than imports — whose profits flowed to the mother country.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — free trade with all nations is the opposite of mercantilist control.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — that was the later French Physiocratic view, not mercantilism.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — non-interference is laissez-faire, the doctrine mercantilism opposed.
option_explanations.D: Right — colonies served the mother country's favorable trade balance.

items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms — Mercantilism: 'the economic doctrine that colonies existed to enrich the mother country through a favorable balance of trade'

items.stem: Thomas Mun, an English merchant, wrote the passage below in 1664. According to Mun, what must a kingdom do to increase its wealth and treasure?

stimulus.text: The ordinary means therefore to increase our wealth and treasure is by Forraign Trade, wherein wee must ever observe this rule; to sell more to strangers yearly than wee consume of theirs in value.
stimulus.attribution: Thomas Mun, England's Treasure by Forraign Trade (1664). Text verified verbatim from the 1664 edition via the Fordham Internet History Sourcebooks.

options: (A) Conquer colonies and seize their gold directly by force.
(B) Sell more to foreigners each year than it buys from them.
(C) Refuse to trade with any foreign nation.
(D) Enrich itself through gifts and payments received from other nations.
items.explanation: Mun's rule is the classic statement of mercantilism: wealth grows through a trade surplus. Sell more abroad than you buy, and the difference comes home as treasure — gold and silver flowing into the kingdom.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — Mun's means is trade, not conquest.
option_explanations.B: Right — 'to sell more to strangers yearly than wee consume of theirs in value.'
option_explanations.C: Wrong — refusing trade would end the exports his whole argument depends on.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — he explicitly dismisses gifts as 'uncertain and of small consideration.'

items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms — Mercantilism: 'the economic doctrine that colonies existed to enrich the mother country through a favorable balance of trade'; stimulus is Mun's 1664 formulation of that doctrine (public domain)

items.stem: Mun illustrated his rule with these figures for England's yearly trade. In his argument, what does the £200,000 'net gain' bar represent?

stimulus.caption: Thomas Mun's numerical example of a favorable balance of trade (1664).

chart_spec.title: Mun's example: England's yearly trade
chart_spec.source_note: Figures from Thomas Mun, England's Treasure by Forraign Trade (1664), ch. 2 — a public-domain primary source: exports £2,200,000, imports £2,000,000, yearly enrichment £200,000

options: (A) The total value of all English trade conducted with other nations that year.
(B) Money that England lost to its foreign competitors.
(C) How much exports exceeded imports: England's yearly gain in treasure.
(D) Taxes collected by the Crown on goods imported from the colonies.
items.explanation: Mun's arithmetic is the doctrine in numbers: £2.2 million of exports minus £2.0 million of imports leaves £200,000 that 'must be brought to us in so much Treasure.' The net gain bar is the surplus itself — the yearly enrichment a favorable balance produces.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — total trade would be exports plus imports, not the difference.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the £200,000 is a gain to England, not a loss.
option_explanations.C: Right — the surplus of exports over imports, converted into treasure.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the example is about the trade balance, not tax collection.

items.fact_source: Stimulus figures from Thomas Mun, England's Treasure by Forraign Trade (1664), ch. 2 (public domain); u2.md §Key terms — Mercantilism: favorable balance of trade

items.stem: The Navigation Acts of the 1660s required colonial trade to be carried on English ships and routed through English ports. Under mercantilist doctrine, what was the purpose of these laws?
options: (A) To make sure colonial trade profits enriched England rather than its rivals.
(B) To encourage colonists to trade directly with France and Spain instead of England.
(C) To end all trade between England and its colonies entirely.
(D) To give colonial assemblies control over imperial trade policy.
items.explanation: The Acts were mercantilism in action: by forcing colonial goods onto English ships through English ports, England captured the shipping profits, the customs duties, and the re-export business — keeping the wealth of colonial trade inside the empire.

option_explanations.A: Right — channeling trade through England kept its profits English.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the Acts were designed to exclude rivals like France and Spain, not invite them.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the Acts regulated and redirected trade; they did not end it.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the Acts asserted imperial control; they gave assemblies nothing.

items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms — Navigation Acts: 'English laws (beginning 1651, tightened in the 1660s) requiring colonial trade to use English ships and pass through English ports'; Mercantilism: 'colonies existed to enrich the mother country'

items.stem: England passed the Navigation Acts to control colonial trade, yet for decades it practiced 'salutary neglect' — loosely enforcing those laws. What does this combination best illustrate about mercantilism in practice?
options: (A) That England had no economic interest in its colonies at all.
(B) That the Navigation Acts were never actually passed by Parliament and existed only as proposals.
(C) That salutary neglect brought all colonial trade with England to a complete and permanent end.
(D) That mercantilist law claimed control on paper while colonial merchants enjoyed wide freedom.
items.explanation: Policy on paper and policy in practice diverged. The Acts asserted England's right to control colonial commerce, but lax enforcement let colonial merchants trade as they pleased and let assemblies grow confident managing their own affairs — the gap between the two is the essence of salutary neglect.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the Acts themselves prove England's strong economic interest.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the Acts were real laws, beginning in 1651 and tightened in the 1660s.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — trade flourished under neglect; it did not end.
option_explanations.D: Right — tight law on paper, loose enforcement in practice.

items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms — Navigation Acts; Salutary neglect: 'Britain's long habit of loosely enforcing its colonial trade and governance laws, which let assemblies grow powerful'; u2.md §What the exam tests here — 'Imperial control vs. colonial autonomy'

items.explanation: Forcing trade through specific ports concentrated commerce there: colonial tobacco, sugar, and rice flowed out through port cities while English manufactured goods flowed in. Merchants in those ports grew rich handling both directions — the review notes colonial merchants prospering on imported English goods.
items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms — Navigation Acts: 'requiring colonial trade to use English ships and pass through English ports'; u2.md §The story — 'merchants to grow rich on imported English goods'

option_explanations.B: Wrong — the Acts redirected trade; they did not ban it.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the laws favored ports, not inland towns.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the Acts restricted trade to English channels; they did not open it to all nations.

options: (A) Ports grew as bottlenecks for colonial exports and English imports, enriching merchants.

items.explanation: The chain runs from the plantation: rice and tobacco needed large labor forces, enslaved labor filled that need, and the transatlantic slave trade supplied the workers. Plantation demand is what made the Middle Passage crossing — and the Africa-to-Americas leg — so massive.

option_explanations.B: Wrong — rice and tobacco were American plantation crops, not African ones.

items.explanation: The review frames the period as a tension: mercantilist law claimed colonial trade for England, while salutary neglect let assemblies and merchants operate freely. That unresolved tension — control on paper, autonomy in practice — is exactly what would snap when Britain later enforced its laws strictly.

option_explanations.B: Wrong — colonists grew more English in taste and merchants grew rich on imported English goods.
option_explanations.C: Right — mercantilist control versus colonial autonomy is the period's central imperial tension.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — mercantilist policy continued; enforcement, not the doctrine, is what changed.
